overview: The island kingdom of Sicily was governed for much of this interval within the Spanish monarchy, usually through a viceroy. Eighteenth-century wars brought Savoyard and Austrian rule before the Bourbons gained the island. Its parliament, ports, grain supply and cities had their own histories; Sicily was not simply another name for Naples.

periods.title: Sicily under the Spanish monarchy
periods.summary: Viceregal government connected the island to wider Spanish dynastic and military commitments.

periods.title: Successive dynastic transfers
periods.summary: The island passed through Savoyard and Austrian control before Bourbon conquest in the 1730s.

periods.title: Bourbon Sicily
periods.summary: Sicily and Naples shared Bourbon rulers while remaining separate kingdoms.

sections.title: Food, trade and the working city

items.text: Messina’s sixteenth-century silk industry had a specialized consulate, granted in 1520, while the harbor served trade and major fleet expeditions. Silk merchants and textile workers lived in a port whose commercial opportunities could be entangled with military demands.

Sicily exported grain while its own towns needed reliable bread supplies. Urban provisioning bodies organized wheat and flour distribution, baking contracts and regulated prices. A grain-producing island could still face arguments over who received the harvest and what a loaf should cost.

The western and central producing regions supplied other parts of Sicily as well as foreign buyers. Export permits issued through the Maestro Portulano could themselves be traded. The journey from field to loaf therefore passed through officials and markets, not only millstones and ovens.

Palermo bought the great Pretoria fountain in 1573 after it had been made for a Florentine garden. Moving a monumental artwork gave the city a new civic centerpiece. What now seems inseparable from one town can have a history that began in another.

During the plague of 1575 to 1576, physician Giovanni Filippo Ingrassia helped organize isolation and health facilities in Palermo. Isolation was not his invention: historians identify earlier use. His importance lay in how medical advice and civic administration were brought together during a crisis.

Research on that epidemic also examines the coercive side of public-health measures: movement and behavior were controlled by authorities. The authors interpret this partly as social control. That is a historical argument, not proof that disease prevention was merely a pretext or that patients had modern rights.

The earthquake of 1693 devastated southeastern towns. Rebuilding was not identical everywhere: Catania largely used its old site, while Noto was created on a new one. Surviving street plans therefore record decisions made after a disaster, as well as architects’ tastes.

At Ragusa and Palazzolo Acreide new urban centers developed beside older ones; Caltagirone was repaired. Together the towns preserve a remarkable concentration of late Baroque buildings. The achievement was collective reconstruction by communities, builders and patrons, not the work of one ruler with one plan.

Prisoners in Palermo’s Inquisition jail left drawings and words on the walls. These surviving graffiti preserve voices from confinement that official case files cannot fully replace. Their later rescue and conservation matter: the marks survived because people chose not to erase them.

Palermo’s first teaching garden for medicinal plants was planted in 1780 on a former powder-magazine site near Porta Carini. It belonged to the new academy’s teaching program. The larger botanical garden visited today came later, so the two sites should not be confused.

A reform at Catania in 1779 expanded teaching, including a chair of experimental physics. The university’s history contrasts this with the earlier dominance of Aristotelian natural philosophy. Learning about nature increasingly involved dedicated experimental instruction, not simply reading inherited authorities.

Italian, the opening of Ingrassia’s printed book title (Palermo, 1576): “Informatione del pestifero, et contagioso morbo”. Translation: “Account of the pestilential and contagious disease.” The full title identifies the Palermo and Sicilian epidemic of 1575 to 1576. This is an attested book title, with its older spelling retained.

ending.text: The map’s 1783 endpoint is not a Sicilian collapse. The Bourbon island kingdom continued through the Napoleonic era and was formally joined with Naples in the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies in 1816.
